title: The Column
standfirst: Seven labs, one row, and a page tree that agreed to lie down sideways.
masthead: Six pieces on the column system, written out of what the labs actually measured. Read them in order or pick one; the row keeps everything you opened.

articles.title: The Row Is the Page
articles.standfirst: One call, and every child of a page becomes a full-height column that opens beside its parent. The tree is real; only the boxes go away.

body.p: A file tree is a hierarchy and a screen is a plane, and the whole argument about navigation is between those two facts. Click into a folder and the folder you were in disappears. Go back and the one you opened does. The information is nested; the reading is not.

`columns()` is one line in a page and it says: from here down, my subtree is a row. Every descendant keeps its place in the tree — its parent, its url, its crumb — and gives up only its box. `display: contents` deletes a wrapper from the layout without deleting it from the document, so a page five levels deep is a peer on screen and a child in the DOM.

body.h: Peers on screen, a tree in the document

body.p: That distinction is the whole design. The visibility contract never changed: a column closes because it lost its mark, not because something moved it. Nothing is re-parented, nothing is re-rendered, and a cold load straight at a five-deep url draws the identical row you would have reached by clicking down to it.

body.caption: Three states of one row: the cover alone, the cover and the contents, and the two of them with this article open beside.

body.quote: A column is not a panel. It is a page that agreed to be narrow.

body.p: What you are reading is that row. The cover is still open to the left — the same page it was when it filled the screen, one rule narrower. The contents beside it never closed. Nothing here is a modal, an overlay or a state machine: it is a handful of pages in a tree, and a stylesheet that decided to stand them side by side.

articles.title: Full Replaces, Fill Joins
articles.standfirst: Six width words, and between two of them the entire vocabulary of a full-screen experience.

body.p: A column asks for its width with one word. `small` is a fixed rail. `hug` fits its own labels. `large` opens to sixty-four ems for a grid or a table. The default is a reading track between sixteen and forty ems. Two words are left, and they are the interesting ones.

`full` takes the whole row and folds every ancestor into the crumb strip above it, so a screen you open with `full` hides the screen you were on. `fill` takes everything left over and keeps its neighbours; the columns already open divide the room evenly. The difference between them is two values.

body.h: Eight experiments, and nothing else was needed

body.p: The pair was tested against every shape a full-screen navigation is usually built from — a title slide, a deck, a two-up divide, a quadrant menu, an uneven pair — and every one of them turned out to be a width word on a page rather than a shell around it. No fixed positioning, no viewport units, no second router.

body.quote: A screen here is not a shell. It is a column that happens to be the only one open.

body.p: Which means Back, the crumb strip and every url keep working exactly as they do three columns deep — because they are three columns deep.

The cover of this issue is `full`. It collapsed the rail you arrived on, and the moment you opened the contents it gave up the major share of the row and stayed. Same page, no second render: one rule that asks whether it has a child open.

articles.title: Forty Ems
articles.standfirst: The oldest number in typography, defended against a monitor that would very much like to spend it.

body.p: A reading column here stops at forty ems, and that ceiling is not a compromise. It is the measure: sixty-odd characters to the line, the width at which the eye finds the start of the next line without hunting for it. This paragraph is sitting on it.

The pressure on it comes from empty space. A column browser on a wide monitor with one page open leaves most of the row grey, and grey reads as broken. The obvious fix is to let the open column absorb the rest.

body.h: It was implemented, and the answer is no

body.p: One selector, and the numbers do close — dead space at 3840 fell from 93% to 68%. It closed them by handing a fourteen-em nav rail eleven hundred pixels, putting a chevron nine hundred pixels from its own label, and giving one sentence a line well past the measure. It traded the thing the width words exist for, and it did not even close the void.

body.quote: Widening a column is never the fix for dead space.

body.p: The two real answers are both declarations. A page that genuinely has something to spend the room on asks for a wider word. A host that would otherwise arrive empty names the child it opens with. Whatever is still left over is drawn as the column slots it already is — a hairline every fourteen ems, saying more opens here.
This article is the default track, and on a wide screen it is deliberately not the widest thing on the row.

articles.title: A Ladder of Paper
articles.standfirst: Four background schemes across three depths, and only one of them reads as depth.

body.p: The same three-column tree, four colour schemes, one question: which of them tells a reader how deep they are without a label?

Stepping the tone up — each column a shade cleaner than the one before — reads as a stack of cards lifting toward you. Stepping down reads as a well you are falling into: the same information with the wrong feeling attached to it.

Alternating fails outright. Depth three matches depth one, so the eye sees a pattern instead of a direction and stops counting. Inverting a single column says this one is different, which is emphasis rather than depth — save it for a column that genuinely is.

body.caption: This issue is the winning scheme, three rungs. The cover behind you carries the most veil; the contents carries less; the article carries none.

body.quote: Never a shadow for a colour. Stacking a translucent well darkens by depth and bands the whole row.

body.p: The page you are reading is the top rung. It is the only white thing on the row, and that is the only reason you can tell at a glance which column is the one you are in.

articles.title: By the Numbers
articles.standfirst: Every width word, measured on the live page at four viewports. Pick a screen and watch them move.

body.p: Numbers first, in pixels, measured headless on the running site rather than computed from the tokens. `row` is the host's whole scroller; the six words below it are what a single column got inside that row.

Read the last two rows together at 3440 and you have the whole of `fill`: `large` stops at its sixty-four-em ceiling and leaves the rest as empty slots, `fill` takes everything the rails did not. At 1920 they are the same number, because `large` has not reached its ceiling yet and nothing else is asking.
Under thirty-two ems of row the arrangement pages one column at a time, which is why every word measures the same at 400.

articles.title: The Empty Room
articles.standfirst: A column browser that has opened one column leaves most of its row grey. What to do about that turned out to be a question about honesty.

body.p: Measured on every columns host on the site: 80% of the row empty at 1280, and 93% at 3840. A flat grey field reads as a page that failed to render, and the reader's first thought is not more opens here.

Absorb was tried and rejected — the previous article has the numbers. What shipped instead moves nothing, measures nothing and builds no DOM. The leftover is drawn as the column slots it already is: one repeating gradient, a hairline every fourteen ems, and an opaque floor under the real bodies so the ghost lines cannot paint through them.

A scrolled row has no leftover and never shows one. A phone, where the row pages a single column at a time, never shows one either. The drawing appears exactly when there is something to say, and says exactly that.

body.quote: The screen now says more opens here instead of nothing rendered.

body.p: Two seams came back into the framework from these labs, and both arrived by occurring three times rather than by being a good idea. A column whose content already shows its children can leave the automatic rail out with one word. And a column a host builds for itself is handed the app it was never routed to receive.
That is the end of issue one. The row is still behind you, and the cover is one click along the crumb strip.
